nutrient-calories-role: Your body needs calories to do things. Your calorie reserve is refilled over time by macro-nutrients such as Fats, Protein, and Carbs. If your calorie reserve reaches zero, your body will begin to starve.
nutrient-protein-role: Protein is needed to build and maintain muscle mass. It is processed and absorbed very differently by your body, and a specific amount must be ingested every 24 hours to meet your goals. Past 64g in a day, each extra gram gives you a little less, and past 128g only half. Protein provides 4kcal per gram (g) when absorbed.
nutrient-carbohydrate-role: Carbs make up the majority of most diets. They are quickly processed by your body into Calories, but cannot be stored for very long and have quickly diminishing returns if eaten too quickly. Carbs provide 4kcal per gram (g) when absorbed.
nutrient-fat-role: Fats are much slower to process but provide your body with more consistent energy over time. You can store a lot more fats in your reserve than any other macro-nutrient. Fats provide 9kcal per gram (g) when absorbed.
nutrient-fiber-role: Fiber keeps your digestion moving and confers absorption rate buffs to each of your macro-nutrients. Keep your daily Fiber intake above 70% to get the best benefits.
nutrient-vitaminK-role: Lets blood clot and wounds close.

guide-overview-text:
Eating Well
A full stomach is not the same as a good diet

Every food now carries real-world nutrition: calories, carbs, fats, protein and fiber, four fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K), vitamin C, the B vitamins, and three minerals (calcium, iron and potassium). Hover over a food to see its calories and how much it fills you, and hold Ctrl to see everything one portion of it contains (or one serving of a bowl or pie). To always see everything, switch off Short food tooltips in the settings. Amounts are shown in grams and kcal, and in mg or mcg for vitamins and minerals.

Your body keeps track of each of these fourteen nutrients. Open the character screen (characterdialog) to see them under Nutritional Reserves, where the five food group bars used to be. Each block on a bar is one day's worth. Hovering over a bar shows how much you have, how long it will last and what the nutrient does. Typing /cnutrition stats in chat lists them all, and the nutrition window (complexnutrition-window) shows everything in one place.

Fullness and Calories
Fullness is how much your stomach holds, out of 600 fullness. It decides how much more you can eat, and it empties within 6 hours whatever you do. What keeps you alive is your calorie reserve, shown by the bar next to your hotbar. It holds about ten days of hard work. Digestion fills it and activity burns it, and when it runs dry you start to starve. The other reserves show whether what you eat is any good. A stomach full of bread will keep you going, but it won't keep your vitamin C up.

While nutrient tracking is turned on, the five vanilla food group bars and the bonus health they give are switched off completely. Only one nutrition system can run at a time. Switching off Nutrient tracking in the settings will adjust your nutrition values to their vanilla equivalents. Be warned that switching Complex Nutrition Tracking back on will set your nutrient values back to the state they were in before the system was toggled off.

For now, calories and fiber are the only nutrients with an effect in game. The effects of a good or poor diet will arrive in a later version.

Read on: Digestion, Nutrient Reserves, How Food Is Counted and The Fourteen Nutrients and The Nutrition Window.
guide-reserves-text:
Nutrient Reserves
Measured in days

Reserves are shown as amounts: kcal for calories, grams for carbs, fats, protein and fiber, and mg or mcg for vitamins and minerals. The B vitamins are a mix of six, so they are shown as a percentage of a day's need. Each reserve also tells you how many days it would last if you stopped eating that nutrient altogether, and each block on its bar is one day.

To see every amount as a percentage of a day's need instead, tooltips included, choose Percent under Amounts or percent in the settings (see The Nutrition Window). Each player picks for themselves, and the server's choice is the default.

Daily Needs
An active day burns about 2,800kcal. You need at least 64g of protein every 24 hours, and your body can use up to 128g. Fiber's daily need is 30g. Carbs and fats have no daily need of their own, because your body simply turns them into calories. Vitamins and minerals use the adult daily values printed on real food labels: vitamin A 900mcg, vitamin D 20mcg, vitamin E 15mg, vitamin K 120mcg, vitamin C 90mg, calcium 1,300mg, iron 18mg and potassium 4,700mg.

Using It Up
Vitamins, minerals and fiber each use up one day's worth per in-game day, whether you are awake or asleep. Calories burn with activity. Standing still burns about 700kcal a day and moving all day burns about 2,800kcal. Sprinting, the cold and anything else that would have raised your vanilla hunger rate will cause you to burn more calories. Carbs, fats and protein are not stored in the same way. They sit in your gut until they are digested into calories, and the Stats panel shows how much is still being digested. Nothing is used up in creative mode or while you are logged out.

How Much the Body Can Store
• Calories: up to 10 active days (28,000kcal), which is a store of body fat. A new character starts with 5 days' worth on a Normal start. The Starting Calories setting, on the Complex Nutrition tab when you create a world, can give a new character anything from a full reserve down to almost nothing, and the Respawn Calories setting does the same for coming back after dying (1 day's worth, Brutal, unless changed).
• Vitamins A, D, E and K: up to 25 days (22,500mcg of vitamin A, for example). Running low takes a long time, and so does recovering.
• Calcium, iron and potassium: up to 10 days (180mg of iron, for example).
• Vitamin C, the B vitamins and fiber: up to 2 days (180mg of vitamin C, for example). These are the first to run low.

Vitamin and mineral stores start at the same share as the calorie reserve: full on a Full start, 70% on Easy, half on Normal, 30% on Hard, 10% on Brutal and next to nothing on Rock Bottom. A Normal start gives 12 and a half days of vitamin A and 5 days of iron, for example. Respawning after dying sets them the same way, from the Respawn Calories setting. A new character always starts with one day of fiber, and a respawned one with none.

Anything eaten past a full store is lost.

See also: Digestion and How Food Is Counted.
guide-counting-title: Complex Nutrition: How Food Is Counted
guide-counting-text:
How Food Is Counted
Every ingredient counts

Single Foods
Each food has the weight of a real-world portion, and its nutrition comes from real food data for that weight. Spoiling food gives less fullness and fewer nutrients in the same measure, and rot gives nothing. How full a food makes you depends on its weight, not its calories (see Digestion).

Meals
A serving from the cooking pot counts as the sum of its ingredients. Cooking makes food easier to digest but destroys some vitamins. A cooked meal gives about 20% more carbs and 10% more protein than its raw ingredients, so more calories, but only half the vitamin C and three quarters of the B vitamins. Each slot of a cooking pot holds up to 10 of an ingredient (vanilla allows 6), for meals of up to 10 servings, which helps with all the small mushrooms you now find. With the Poultry and bushmeat in pots setting switched on, raw, cooked and cured poultry and bushmeat also go into meat stews and soups. Crock pot contents are simply preserved and receive no nutritional losses or buffs from storage.

Pies and Bread
A pie's calories and nutrients include the values from both its filling and its crust. A slice is a quarter of the pie's total value. Charred or part-baked pies and bread lose a lot of their nutrition.

Drinks
Drinks provide their full nutritional benefit but at half the fullness rate, enabling you to take in a lot more. They are an excellent source and store of most vitamins. A sip a day keeps the scurvy away!

Large Meals
Your body can only take in so much of each nutrient at once. Carbs, fats and protein give fewer calories once you have digested a lot of them in a short time (see Digestion). Fiber, vitamins and minerals work in a similar way. Everything you eat within an hour of your last food is added together, and up to a day and a half's worth of each nutrient is taken in fully. Past that, each extra day's worth only adds about two thirds of a day to your reserve. Spreading rich foods out and eating a mix of them works better than one big feast.

Mushrooms
Every mushroom species has its own nutrient profile. All of them are light and low in calories, but some are worth the hunt. Morels are rich in iron, and chanterelles and morels both carry vitamin D. Woody brackets such as reishi and tinder hoof are mostly fiber. Each mushroom weighs about what a real one would. Mushrooms that grow in clusters give you several at once, so a patch of morels or liberty caps gives four to eight small mushrooms, while a king bolete or an oyster mushroom gives one big one. Poisonous species still have their nutrients, and they will still poison you.

Wild Crops
Crops growing wild give less than the same crop grown on farmland. By default a wild crop gives half of a farmed harvest, so a wild spelt plant gives 2 to 4 grain. In vanilla it is a quarter. An admin can change this under World in the settings menu.

Foods from Other Mods
Foods without nutrition data of their own are estimated from their food group and vanilla satiety. Full support for other mods is planned, and modders can add their nutrient profiles using the template included with this mod's release files. Complex Nutrition will automatically import these when loading the world.

See also: The Fourteen Nutrients.
guide-digestion-text:
Digestion
From stomach to calorie reserve

Fullness
Your stomach holds 600 fullness, which is about 2 kilograms of food. Every food fills you by its weight: an apple fills 54 fullness, a loaf of bread 54 fullness and a whole cabbage 270 fullness. Meals, pies and anything cooked, baked, smoked or cured fill you 20% less, so cooking lets you eat more at once. Drinks fill you half as much as their weight would. Fullness drains by 100 every hour, whatever you are doing, so a full stomach is empty in 6 hours. It only decides whether you can eat. Food that doesn't fit has to wait, and an empty stomach does you no harm.

The Gut
Whatever you eat goes into your gut and is digested over the next few hours. The more of something your gut holds, the faster it absorbs it, up to a limit. A well-filled gut works at full speed, and a nearly empty one slows to a trickle. The times below are for one serving eaten on its own, and a fuller gut gets through more in the same time:
• Carbs (not counting their fiber) are absorbed at up to 90g an hour, so 100g takes about 3 hours. Your gut holds up to 500g at a time.
• Protein is absorbed at up to 15g an hour, so 40g takes about 5 and a half hours. Your gut holds up to 200g at a time.
• Fats are absorbed at up to 6g an hour, so 70g takes about a day. With more fat in your gut it goes faster, up to about 135g a day. Your gut holds up to 240g at a time.

Anything eaten past a full gut passes straight through and is wasted.

Your body can only make good use of so much of each macro-nutrient at once, so eating more than that gives diminishing returns. Every gram you digest counts towards a running total. Once that total passes a certain amount, each extra gram gives you fewer calories than the last:
• Carbs: past 300g digested in 12 hours. Three meals of about 130g each, six hours apart, stay under it, but a single 400g feast goes over.
• Fats: past 70g digested in 24 hours, so eating more than about 70g of fat a day goes over.
• Protein: past 64g digested in 24 hours, each gram gives a little less, sliding down to 80% of its calories by 128g. Every gram past 128g gives only half its calories.

The totals fall again as the hours pass, so spreading your meals across the day works better than one big feast. An admin can switch diminishing returns off for the whole world under World in the settings menu, and then every gram counts in full.

Calories
Digestion is the only thing that fills your calorie reserve. Each gram of carbs or protein gives 4kcal and each gram of fats gives 9kcal. The reserve holds 10 active days and activity burns it. The bar next to your hotbar shows it, one block per day, and flashes when it falls below a tenth. As long as there is anything in it you heal at full speed, however full your stomach is, and healing uses up calories from it. A recovering body needs 33 to 44kcal per kg a day instead of about 25, so each health point you heal on your own costs about 22kcal when you are barely hurt and up to about 53kcal when you are badly hurt. The more damage you take, the more it costs to heal. Healing items cost nothing. When it is empty you stop healing and starve, losing health until you eat. After dying you come back with what the Respawn Calories setting gives (a day's worth unless changed), with an empty gut and no fiber.

Fiber
When your fiber reserve is at 70% of a day's need or more, digestion runs faster: fats by 30%, protein by 20% and carbs by 10%. The bonus shrinks as the reserve runs down. The fiber bar's hover and the Overview tab of the nutrition window show how many extra calories an hour this is helping you digest right now. In real life fiber tends to slow digestion down a little, but here it is a reward for eating your greens.

What This Means
A stomach full of stew gives about 2,000kcal, a stomach full of bread over 6,000kcal, and a stomach full of mushrooms very little. Fruit and vegetables alone won't carry a hard-working day, so add meat, grain, bread or cheese.

See also: Nutrient Reserves and How Food Is Counted.
guide-nutrients-text:
The Fourteen Nutrients
What they do and where to find them

Calories and fiber are the only nutrients with an effect on your character so far, and carbs, fats and protein are what your body makes calories from. Every other nutrient will get its own effect in a later version, even if a small one. Until then, its entry below says In game: planned.

Calories: your body needs calories to do things. Your calorie reserve is refilled over time by macro-nutrients such as carbs, fats and protein. If it reaches zero, your body will begin to starve. The richest foods are fat, butter, honey, nuts and bread. In game: an empty reserve starves you.
Carbs: carbs make up the majority of most diets. They are quickly turned into calories, but they can't be stored for very long and have quickly diminishing returns if you eat too much of them too quickly. Carbs give 4kcal per gram once absorbed. Grains, bread, honey and cassava. In game: a typical serving is digested into calories within about 3 hours.
Fats: fats are much slower to process, but they give your body more consistent energy over time. You can store a lot more fats than any other macro-nutrient. Fats give 9kcal per gram once absorbed, and they are needed to take in vitamins A, D, E and K. Animal fat, butter, walnuts, peanuts, cheese and sunflower seeds. In game: a typical serving is digested into calories over about 24 hours.
Protein: protein is needed to build and maintain muscle mass. Your body processes and absorbs it very differently from carbs and fats, and you need to eat a certain amount of it every 24 hours. Past 64g in a day each extra gram gives a little less, and past 128g only half. Protein gives 4kcal per gram once absorbed. Meat, fish, cheese, soybeans and peanuts. In game: a typical serving is digested into calories within about 6 hours. Muscle is planned.
Fiber: fiber keeps your digestion moving and speeds up how quickly each of your macro-nutrients is absorbed. Keep your fiber reserve above 70% to get the best benefit. Flax, rye, soybeans, peanuts and berries. In game: speeds up digestion.
Vitamin C: healing, and healthy gums. Sailors who went without it got scurvy. Blackcurrants, cloudberries, bell peppers, strawberries and oranges. Cooking destroys some of it. In game: planned.
B vitamins: they turn food into energy. Meat, fish, soybeans, peanuts and sunflower seeds. In game: planned.
Vitamin A: eyesight and skin. Carrots, butter, pumpkin and cheese. In game: planned.
Vitamin D: strong bones, together with calcium. Smoked and cured fish, chanterelles, morels and eggs. In game: planned.
Vitamin E: protects the body's cells. Sunflower seeds, peanuts and olives. In game: planned.
Vitamin K: lets blood clot and wounds close. Cabbage, fennel, soybeans, parsnips, blackberries and blueberries. In game: planned.
Calcium: bones and teeth. Cheese, soybeans, milk and flax. In game: planned.
Iron: carries oxygen in the blood. Soybeans, morels, bushmeat, olives and amaranth. In game: planned.
Potassium: keeps muscles and nerves working. Soybeans, fish, cattail and papyrus roots, and peanuts. In game: planned.

See also: Nutrient Reserves.

guide-window-text:
The Nutrition Window
Everything in one place

Press complexnutrition-window (Left Alt + N unless you have changed it in the controls menu), or the Details button on the Stats panel, to open the nutrition window. It is the same size as the handbook and can stay open while you play. It keeps itself up to date every second.

Overview
Your calorie reserve and fullness, how many calories the food in your gut will still give and how many of them are being lost to diminishing returns, the calories you burned in the last hour, day and week, what healing is costing you while you are hurt, how much carbs, fats and protein you have digested lately against the point where they start giving fewer calories, how many extra calories an hour fiber is helping you digest right now, and a Running Low list. The calorie reserve shows up there when it falls under a day. Vitamins A, D, E and K and the minerals show up when they fall under two days, because they take a long time to build back up. Carbs, fats, protein, fiber, vitamin C and the B vitamins refresh so quickly that they get no warning. Each nutrient on the list comes with the best foods for it, picked only from foods you have held at some point.

Digestion
What is in your stomach and gut, how many calories it will still give, how long it will take, how fast it is being absorbed, and how much fiber is speeding things up.

Vitamins and Minerals
Every vitamin and mineral, how much you have stored, how many days it will last, what it does and the best foods you know for it. Days turn amber when a slow nutrient is running low and red when it is nearly gone. An arrow beside each bar shows whether that store went up (green), held steady (grey) or went down (amber) over the last day.

History
The last 28 days. The first chart shows the calories digestion added to your reserve each day (green) against the calories you burned (red). Under it, how much you ate and spent a day over the last week, and where most of your food came from. The Calories by Food Type chart has a bar for the calories you ate each day, coloured by food group, and the dashed line marks a day's need. Its white line shows one store at the end of each day: your calorie reserve, fiber, or any vitamin or mineral, picked from the list at the bottom of the window. Days you weren't playing are left blank.

Settings
The Settings button at the bottom of the window (or typing /cnutrition settings) opens the settings. Every player can change the Display settings: the advanced nutrition display, and whether amounts are shown as amounts or as a percentage of a day's need. Admins (and you, in single player) also get Food Info, World and Modules: food tooltips, starting and respawn calories, diminishing returns, how much wild crops give, poultry and bushmeat in pots, and switching each part of the mod on or off. Every player can also switch off Short food tooltips and the Running Low icon. Switching Nutrient tracking off or on asks you to confirm first, because it changes everyone's nutrition at once. Hover over a setting's name to see what it does.

The Running Low Icon
A small bowl to the right of your hotbar. It turns amber when something on the Running Low list is low and red when something is nearly gone or your calorie reserve is under a day. Click it to open the nutrition window.

See also: Eating Well.
